Two images frame the collection

Verse 1 uses three verbs that slow down: walk, stand, sit. A person drifts, then stops, then settles among scoffers. Verse 3 answers with a tree that has been planted by water. It does not find the stream by chance. Its fruit comes “in its season,” so not at every moment. Chaff in verse 4 has no root and no weight. The poem sets these two pictures at the gate of the whole collection.
Royal language ends with a warning

The poem has four voices: the rebels, God, the king, and the poet. Verse 9 threatens the nations with a rod of iron. Verse 10 follows that threat with an offer. Kings and judges are addressed as students who can still learn. The last line blesses all who take refuge. Psalm 1 began with “Blessed,” and Psalm 2 ends with it. Acts 4:25–26 and Hebrews 1:5 apply this poem to Jesus.
Sleep becomes evidence of endurance

The danger in verse 1 is still there in verse 6. The enemies have not left. Between those verses the speaker sleeps. Verse 5 treats that sleep as evidence. A man hunted by thousands lay down and woke up safe. He gives the reason in the same verse: the LORD sustains him. Second Samuel 15–17 tells of the night flight the heading names.
Joy uses a different measure

Verse 6 quotes a common question: who will show us any good? The people asking it measure good by grain and new wine. Verse 7 compares two kinds of gladness. Theirs rises when the harvest increases. His has been “put” in his heart by God. It does not depend on the size of a crop. Verse 8 ends with sleep, as Psalm 3 did with waking.
Morning organizes a waiting prayer

Verse 3 says “in the morning” twice. The speaker lays out his requests in order, as one sets out an offering. Then he watches. Prayer here has two parts: careful asking and expectant waiting. Verse 4 gives his ground for hope: God does not side with evil. His enemies’ main weapon is the mouth (verse 9). Romans 3:13 quotes that verse.
Tears give the complaint a place

Verse 3 breaks off: “But you, LORD—how long?” The speaker is too worn to complete it. Verse 6 places his grief in a bed and a couch, at night. Tears are his only words there. In verse 8 his tone changes without any reported event. He says the LORD has heard his weeping. So the poem counts crying itself as a prayer that is heard.
The appeal includes a test of innocence

Verses 3–5 are an oath of innocence. The speaker names possible wrongs and invites the penalty if they are true. Verse 4 concerns repaying a friend with evil. Job uses the same form at length in Job 31. Asking for judgment is a risk, since the judge examines both sides. Verse 8 accepts that risk: “Judge me.” Verses 15–16 expect evil to fall back on the one who planned it.
Smallness and dignity belong together

Verse 3 calls the heavens the work of God’s fingers. Against that scale verse 4 asks what a human is. The question expects the answer “very little.” Verse 5 answers with a crown. Smallness and dignity are held together. The rule over animals in verses 6–8 echoes Genesis 1:26–28. Job 7:17 turns this same question into a complaint.
Public praise includes forgotten people

Thanks and pleading are mixed through this poem. Verse 12 says God does not forget the cry of the afflicted. Verse 18 says the needy will not “always” be forgotten. That word admits they are forgotten now. The hope of the poor is a hope still waiting. Verses 19–20 turn the hope into a request. The nations must learn they are only men.
The enemy’s claim drives the prayer

The poem quotes the oppressor’s private thoughts three times (verses 4, 6, 11). Verse 11 holds his whole plan. God has forgotten, hides his face, and will never see. His cruelty depends on that belief. Verse 1 voices the same worry from the victim’s side. Both think God seems hidden, and they draw opposite conclusions. Verse 14 answers the oppressor directly: “But you do see.”
An offered escape is challenged

Verses 1–3 quote advice given to the speaker. The danger is real, and his friends say to run. Verse 3 is their strongest point: order itself is failing. He does not deny it. Verse 4 looks above the failing foundations to a throne that stands. Verse 5 says the LORD “tests” the righteous. Trouble can be an examination and not a sign of being left.
Words can either exploit or protect

The poem sets two kinds of speech against each other. Human speech in verses 2–4 is flattery, lies, and boasting. The LORD speaks once, in verse 5. His words are a promise to the poor and needy. Verse 6 calls his words silver with no dross left. “Pure” here means fully reliable, unlike the talk around it. Verse 8 ends with the liars still walking about.
Repeated questions stretch the wait

The four questions point in three directions. Verse 1 looks at God, who seems to forget. Verse 2 looks inside, at daily sorrow, and then at the enemy. The whole poem is only six verses long. It moves from complaint to request to trust. Nothing in the situation is said to change. The turn in verse 5 begins with “But I,” and rests on past kindness.
A judgment about humanity becomes social

The fool’s denial in verse 1 is spoken “in his heart.” It is not an argument; it is a way of living. Verse 4 shows what it looks like. Such people devour others as casually as eating bread. They also never pray. The poem ties unbelief to how the weak are treated. Verse 6 names the LORD as the refuge of the poor they shame.
Entry depends on ordinary conduct

The question in verse 1 is about worship. The answer never mentions an offering. Every item concerns how a person treats others. Verse 3 covers the tongue: no slander and no insults. Verse 4 covers promises that have become costly. Verse 5 covers money: no interest and no bribes. Psalm 24:3–4 asks the same question and answers in the same way.
Inheritance gives security a shape

Verse 6 uses the language of dividing land. “Lines” are the cords that marked out each family’s share. Joshua 13–19 describes those shares. The Levites received no land, because the LORD was their portion (Numbers 18:20). The speaker takes that language for himself in verse 5. His share is God. Acts 2:25–28 applies verses 8–11 to the resurrection of Jesus.
Protection becomes intimate

Verse 8 uses two pictures of close protection. The “apple of your eye” is the pupil, the part a person guards by reflex. The “shadow of your wings” is a bird covering its young. Both are near and tender. Verses 11–12 show why he needs them: enemies close in like lions. He makes this request after his heart has been examined (verse 3). Verse 15 sets his hope against people whose share is this life alone.
Rescue is described through an overwhelming landscape

Verses 7–15 describe an earthquake, thunder, hail, and the sea floor laid bare. All of it answers one man’s cry (verse 6). Verse 16 then narrows that power to a single act. A hand reaches down, takes hold, and pulls him from the water. The scale of the storm shows the worth of the one rescued. Verse 19 calls the result “a large place,” the opposite of the cords. Second Samuel 22 gives the same song.
The poem narrows from skies to speech

The poem moves in three steps. Verses 1–6 look at the sky, and verses 7–11 at the LORD’s law. Verses 12–14 look at one person. The view narrows from the universe to a text to a heart. Nothing hides from the sun (verse 6), and the law also exposes. So verse 12 asks about faults he cannot see. Verse 14 offers his mouth and his thoughts for inspection.
A community speaks before a battle

In verses 1–5 the people speak to their king as “you.” In verse 6 one voice says, “Now I know.” Verse 7 then compares two kinds of trust. Chariots and horses were the strongest weapons of the time. Deuteronomy 17:16 told Israel’s king not to build up horses. The people name the LORD’s name as their weapon. Verse 9 asks “the King” to answer, so the human king also has a King.
Royal praise locates strength elsewhere

Psalm 20 asked that the king receive his heart’s desire (20:4). Verse 2 here says God has given it. The two poems form a request and its answer. Verse 7 is the hinge of this one. The king is secure because he trusts and because the Most High is kind. Verse 3 says God set the crown on him. The poem begins and ends with “your strength,” meaning God’s (verses 1 and 13).
A song can move without erasing its beginning

The first line accuses and still says “my God” twice. The speaker complains to the one he feels has left. The poem then swings between pain and memory. Complaint and memory alternate through verses 1–10. From verse 22 it becomes praise. Verse 24 says God has not hidden his face. Jesus speaks the first line on the cross in Mark 15:34.
The shelter changes from field to table

The poem changes its picture at verse 5. The shepherd of verses 1–4 becomes a host with a table. A host’s duties are all there: food, oil for the head, a full cup. The enemies have not gone; the meal is served in front of them. The poem also changes its grammar. “He” becomes “you” in verse 4, in the dark valley. In verse 6 goodness “follows” him, where enemies usually pursue.
Ownership leads to a question about access

Verse 1 says the owner of the whole earth has one hill as his own. Verse 3 asks who may enter there. Verse 4 names hands, heart, and speech. Hands are deeds, the heart is intent, and oaths are words. No offering is mentioned. The questions and answers read like an exchange at a gate (verses 3, 8, 10). Worshipers go up in verse 3, and the King comes in at verse 7.
Memory can wound or restore

The word “remember” comes three times in verses 6–7. God should remember his own mercies, which are ancient. He should not remember the speaker’s early sins. He should remember the speaker himself, according to his kindness. The request is about which memory will govern. Its ground is God’s goodness, not any claim of improvement. Verse 11 even asks for pardon because the guilt is great.
A claim of integrity leads toward worship

Priests washed before they served at the altar (Exodus 30:17–21). Elders washed their hands to declare innocence in Deuteronomy 21:6. Verse 6 draws on that practice. The speaker’s claim to integrity has a goal. He wants to stand at the altar among those who give thanks (verses 7–8). It is not a claim to need nothing. Verse 11 still asks, “Redeem me, and be merciful to me.”
Confidence turns into a request

The first half of the poem is confident (verses 1–6). The second half pleads (verses 7–14). Verse 4 stands in the confident half and is already a request. With armies around him, he asks for “one thing.” It is not victory or even safety. He wants to live near God, look, and ask. The last verse tells him to wait, so the request is not yet granted.
Silence feels like descent

Verse 1 joins two pictures that do not fit: a rock that might be deaf. The speaker’s whole safety rests on being heard. He says God’s silence would be like death, the “pit.” Verse 2 asks God to hear the voice of his pleading. Verse 6 uses the same words to say that God has heard. Nothing else is reported between request and thanks. Verses 8–9 widen the prayer to all the people.
A storm supplies the poem’s repeated voice

“The LORD’s voice” comes seven times in this poem. The voice is thunder, and the poem follows a storm. Verse 3 hears it over the sea. Verses 5–6 see it break trees in Lebanon to the north. Verse 8 follows it into the wilderness. All that power ends in two gifts in verse 11. The last word of the poem is “peace.”
Past security receives a correction

Verse 6 is a confession about the speaker’s good years. He said, “I shall never be moved.” Verse 7 corrects him. His mountain stood firm only by God’s favor. He had taken a gift for his own strength. When God hid his face, the confidence was gone at once. The poem thanks God for a rescue and also for that lesson.
Trust remains inside a threatened life

Verse 13 describes a threat made of talk. He hears slander, and people plan together to take his life. Jeremiah 20:10 uses almost the same words, “terror on every side.” Verse 14 answers with “But I trust in you.” His trust is stated inside the danger, before it ends. Verse 15 places his “times” in God’s hand, against those who plot his end. Jesus speaks verse 5 from the cross in Luke 23:46.
Silence and confession have different bodily effects

Verse 3 describes hidden sin through the body. Bones waste, and groaning lasts all day. Verse 4 adds heat and a heavy hand. Verse 5 uses three verbs of opening up: acknowledge, not hide, confess. Forgiveness follows within the same verse. He had been hiding his sin; in verse 7 God becomes his hiding place. Romans 4:7–8 quotes verses 1–2.
A hymn tests familiar signs of strength

The poem first describes a world made by a word (verses 6–9). It then describes God watching every person from heaven (verses 13–15). Against that background verse 16 looks at military strength. A king’s army, a warrior’s strength, and a horse are the usual grounds of safety. Verses 16–17 say each one fails. Verse 18 names what does not fail: the LORD’s eye on those who wait. Verse 2 calls for a harp; the Egyptian harp shown is a comparison.
Personal testimony becomes instruction

Verses 4–6 give the speaker’s own story. Verse 8 turns it into an invitation. “Taste and see” asks others to test it by experience. In verse 11 he becomes a teacher and calls the young to listen. His lesson is practical: guard speech, do good, pursue peace (verses 13–14). Verse 19 is honest that the righteous have many afflictions. First Peter 3:10–12 quotes verses 12–16.
Friendship intensifies the injury

Verse 13 says the speaker fasted and prayed when these people were ill. Verse 14 says he mourned for them as for his own mother. Verse 15 gives their answer when he fell: they gathered with joy. The wound is betrayal of care he had given. The phrase “without cause” marks the poem (verses 7 and 19). He asks God to judge the matter. He does not describe taking revenge himself.
Two landscapes describe opposing lives

Verses 1–4 describe a small, closed world: one man scheming on his bed. Verses 5–6 open onto sky, mountains, and ocean. Verse 7 then brings that vast kindness close. People shelter under God’s wings as chicks do. The verse says “children of men,” which means humans in general. Verse 6 has already included the animals. Verses 8–9 add a feast, a river, a fountain, and light.
Waiting interrupts envy

The poem tells the reader three times not to “fret” (verses 1, 7, 8). Verse 8 says where fretting leads: to doing evil. So envy of the wicked is the real danger to the righteous. Verse 7 gives the remedy, which is to rest and wait. Verse 10 adds “a little while.” The speaker takes the long view of an old man (verse 25). Psalm 73 and the book of Job test this confidence against harder cases.
Bodily pain and isolation reinforce each other

The poem has three layers of trouble. Verses 3–10 describe the body. Verse 11 says friends and relatives stand far off. Verse 12 says enemies move closer. Sickness has left him alone when he most needs company. He does not answer his accusers and leaves that to God (verses 13–15). Unlike Job he admits his sin (verse 18), and the poem ends still pleading.
Guarded speech turns into a question about life

Verses 1–3 describe a failed attempt at silence. The words he held in burned like fire. What finally comes out in verse 4 is a question about his own end. A handbreadth in verse 5 is the width of four fingers. It was among the smallest measures in use. Verse 6 notes that wealth is gathered for unknown heirs. In verse 12 he calls himself a stranger staying with God.
A rescued voice still needs help

Most prayers of this kind move from trouble to thanks. This one runs the other way. Verses 1–10 give thanks for a rescue already received. Verses 11–17 plead in a new crisis. One rescue has not ended his need. Verse 17 calls him poor and needy, and still the Lord thinks of him. He began by waiting patiently and ends with “don’t delay.”
Illness exposes broken loyalty

Verse 1 blesses anyone who considers the weak. The speaker is now weak, and he meets the opposite. Visitors come to his bedside to collect bad news (verse 6). Verse 9 names the worst case. A trusted friend who shared his bread has turned on him. Sharing a meal was a bond of loyalty. Jesus applies this verse to Judas in John 13:18.
The speaker addresses his own soul

Verse 5 is a refrain that returns in verse 11 and in 43:5. In it the speaker talks to himself. One part of him asks the other why it is so low. He does not deny the despair. He questions it and orders it to hope. The water pictures change through the poem. He begins with thirst (verses 1–2) and ends under a flood (verse 7).
The desired journey begins with guidance

This short poem finishes Psalm 42 and shares its refrain. Verse 3 asks for two guides: light and truth. They are pictured as an escort for a journey home. The route is named in order: hill, dwelling, altar, and God (verses 3–4). The speaker is still far away. Verse 5 repeats the question to his soul a third time. Hope is commanded, and arrival is not yet reported.
Shared suffering challenges a simple explanation

This is a prayer of the whole people after a defeat. Deuteronomy 28 and the book of Judges explain defeat by unfaithfulness. Verse 17 says that explanation does not fit this time. The people claim they have kept the covenant (verses 18–21). Verse 22 says they are killed “for your sake.” Verse 23 dares to ask why God sleeps. Israel kept this protest among its songs of worship.
Royal celebration includes a change of belonging

The first half addresses the king, and verse 10 turns to the bride. The poet asks three things of her: listen, consider, and turn her ear. Then he names the cost. She must forget her people and her father’s house. The wedding is a celebration, and it is also a loss for her. Verse 16 offers sons in the place of fathers. Hebrews 1:8–9 applies verses 6–7 to Christ.
A refuge remains amid upheaval

Verse 9 says God ends wars and destroys weapons. Verse 10 is his voice in that setting. “Be still” is an order to stop. It is spoken to raging nations as much as to worried worshipers. The poem sets two kinds of water side by side. The sea roars in verse 3, and a river runs quietly in verse 4. The refrain in verses 7 and 11 says the LORD of Armies is with them.
Celebration widens beyond one people

Verse 1 speaks to “all you nations,” not to Israel alone. Verse 9 pictures foreign princes assembled. They gather as the people of the God of Abraham. Genesis 12:3 promised blessing for all families through Abraham. “Shields” in this verse means rulers who protect. Verse 3 speaks of nations subdued under Israel. The poem holds both pictures, and it ends with the gathering.
A city becomes something to tell others

Verses 12–13 send the worshipers on a tour of the walls. They count towers and study the ramparts. The purpose comes at the end of verse 13: tell the next generation. The walls are evidence for a story. Verse 3 has already said the refuge is God, not the stone. Verse 14 gives the tour’s conclusion, “this God is our God.” Verse 8 says each generation moves from hearing to seeing.
Death limits wealth’s power

This poem speaks to all humanity, like a proverb (verses 1–2). In Israel’s law money could sometimes ransom a life (Exodus 21:30). Verse 7 says no payment works against death. Verses 8–9 call the price too high for anyone. Verse 14 pictures death as a shepherd leading his flock. Verse 15 then says what people cannot do, God will do. The refrain in verses 12 and 20 compares the proud rich to animals that perish.
A divine speech challenges ownership in worship

The poem is a court scene with God as accuser and judge. Verse 8 says the offerings themselves are not the problem. The problem is the idea that God needs feeding. Verses 10–11 state that he owns every animal already. Verse 12 makes the point with dry humor. What he asks is in verses 14–15: thanks, faithfulness, and a call for help. The people need him; he does not need them.
Confession asks for more than erased guilt

Verses 1–2 and 9 ask God to blot out a record. Verse 10 asks for more than a cleared account. “Create” is the word used for God’s work in Genesis 1:1. The speaker cannot make a clean heart for himself. He asks God to make one. Verse 11 fears losing God’s Spirit, as Saul did (1 Samuel 16:14). Verse 13 expects a forgiven man to become a teacher.
A rooted life answers destructive speech

Verse 5 says the boaster will be uprooted. Verse 8 answers with a tree that stays rooted. An olive tree is evergreen and lives for many generations. This one grows in God’s house. Verse 7 says the powerful man trusted in riches. The speaker trusts in loving kindness. First Samuel 22:9–19 shows what Doeg’s tongue cost the priests of Nob.
Corruption becomes consumption of a people

The book keeps this poem twice, here with the name “God” throughout. Verse 4 holds the charge. The evildoers consume people as an everyday meal. They also do not call on God. Verse 5 is the main difference from Psalm 14. Panic strikes the oppressors when nothing threatens them. The people they frightened are not the ones who end in fear.
A short prayer changes from petition to thanks

This prayer has seven verses, and verse 4 is its hinge. Before it the speaker pleads. After it he speaks as if the rescue were done. Verse 3 says his enemies have not set God before them. In verse 4 he does exactly that with the word “Behold.” Nothing outward has changed between verses 3 and 4. First Samuel 23:19 tells of the betrayal the heading names.
The deepest threat comes from a companion

Verse 12 says he could have endured an enemy or hidden from one. Verse 13 names the real source: “a man like me.” The friend was his equal and knew him well. Verse 14 adds that they worshiped together. This kind of harm makes him want to flee, not fight (verses 6–8). Verse 21 describes speech as smooth as butter that hides a sword. Verse 22 promises he will be sustained, not that the burden goes.
Tears become a request for remembrance

Verse 6 says enemies mark the speaker’s steps in order to kill him. Verse 8 says God also keeps count of his wanderings. The same watching has an opposite purpose. God stores his tears and records them. Nothing he suffers is lost or overlooked. Verse 3 does not deny fear: “When I am afraid.” Verse 9 gives his conclusion: God is for him.
A trap reverses its direction

Verse 6 turns in the middle. The enemies spread a net and dig a pit. Then they fall into it themselves. The poem pauses there. The refrain in verses 5 and 11 lifts the view above the cave. In verse 8 the speaker does not wait for morning. He says he will wake the dawn with his song.
The prayer challenges corrupt judgment

The poem speaks to people whose work is to judge. Verse 2 says they “measure out” violence. A judge should weigh evidence, and these weigh out harm. The curses in verses 6–9 are fierce. They are requests handed to God; they are not actions taken. Verse 11 gives the reason for them. People need to be able to say that someone judges the earth.
Repeated sounds organize the danger

Two refrains shape this poem. Verses 6 and 14 describe the enemies as dogs prowling at evening. Verses 9 and 17 call God “my strength.” The evening belongs to the enemies. Verse 16 gives the morning to the speaker’s song. Verse 11 makes an unusual request. He wants them left alive, so that his people do not forget.
Defeat creates a question about divine presence

Verses 6–8 quote God claiming every region by name. Verse 10 sets a recent defeat against that claim. God has not gone out with the armies. The people hold the promise and the loss together. They do not drop either one. Verse 11 draws the lesson that human help is empty. Verse 12 still expects victory through God.
Distance shapes the request for refuge

Verse 2 places the speaker at “the end of the earth.” He is far from God’s house, or feels that he is. He asks for a rock “higher than I.” It is a height he cannot reach alone, so he says, “Lead me.” Verse 3 gives his reason for asking. God has been a refuge to him before. Verses 6–7 add a prayer for the king.
Quiet trust rejects false sources of security

The word “alone” or “only” runs through verses 1, 2, 5, and 6. Verse 9 removes people of every rank as a support. Verse 10 removes money gained by force or theft. It then adds a harder case. Even if riches simply grow, the heart must not settle on them. Wealth is not condemned, and trust in it is. Verses 11–12 name what remains: God’s power joined with kindness.
Thirst continues through the night

The night was divided into watches for guards. Verse 6 says the speaker lies awake through them, thinking of God. His thirst in verse 1 is met by memory in verse 2. Verse 5 says he is satisfied as with a feast, in a desert. Verse 3 values God’s kindness above life itself. Verse 8 describes holding in both directions. He clings, and God’s hand holds him up.
Speech becomes a hidden weapon

The weapons in verse 3 are words. The attack is secret, sudden, and sure it is unseen (verses 2, 4, 5). The poem treats slander as seriously as violence. Verse 7 answers in the same terms. God shoots an arrow, and it also comes “suddenly.” Verse 8 says their own tongues will ruin them. The harm returns by the road it came.
Praise follows provision across the land

The poem moves in three parts. Verses 1–4 stand in the temple, and verses 5–8 view mountains and seas. Verses 9–13 walk through farmland. Verse 9 pictures God as a farmer visiting his field. He waters it and prepares the grain. Verse 10 follows the rain into the plowed furrows. In verse 13 the land itself shouts and sings.
A public hymn becomes personal testimony

The poem changes speaker at verse 13. Verses 1–12 say “we” and tell the nation’s story. Verses 13–20 say “I.” Verse 5 invites people to “come and see” the great acts of old. Verse 16 invites them to “come and hear” one person’s account. A single life is set beside the crossing of the sea. Verse 18 adds that he did not hold on to wrong in his heart.
A blessing seeks a wider purpose

Verse 1 borrows the priests’ blessing from Numbers 6:24–26. Verse 2 adds a purpose to it with the word “that.” Israel asks to be blessed so that others may know God’s way. The blessing is not meant to stop with those who receive it. The refrain in verses 3 and 5 names “all the peoples.” Verse 6 suggests a harvest as the occasion. The last verse reaches to the ends of the earth.
A procession joins power with care

This is a poem of marching, battle, and procession. Verse 5 says what kind of ruler leads it. In his holy dwelling God is father to the fatherless. He defends widows, who had no one to speak for them. Verse 6 adds homes for the lonely and freedom for prisoners. The poem describes God’s power by naming those it protects. Verse 1 repeats the words spoken when the ark set out (Numbers 10:35).
Ridicule makes suffering publicly visible

The poem opens with drowning, but its deepest wound is shame. Verses 7–12 describe mockery from family, elders, and drunkards. Verse 20 says insult has broken his heart. He looked for comforters and found none, as Job did. Verse 21 shows the only “care” he received: gall and vinegar. The curses in verses 22–28 are handed to God. The Gospels apply verses 9 and 21 to Jesus (John 2:17; Matthew 27:34).
Urgency supplies the poem’s structure

The prayer has only five verses. It begins with “hurry” and ends with “don’t delay.” Verses 3 and 4 divide people by what they say. One group says, “Aha!” The other says, “Let God be exalted.” The speaker has no time for a longer form. These verses also appear at the end of Psalm 40.
Old age changes the request for survival

The speaker names the womb, youth, and gray hair (verses 6, 17, 18). His enemies read his weakness as proof that God has gone (verses 10–11). Verse 18 gives his reason for wanting more time. He has not finished telling the next generation. Verse 20 admits that God let him see many troubles. Verse 22 promises music on the harp and lyre. The Egyptian harp shown is a comparison, not Israel’s instrument.
Royal greatness is measured through vulnerable lives

Verses 8–11 pray for a rule that reaches the ends of the earth. Verse 12 begins with “For” and gives the reason. This king deserves such rule because he rescues the helpless. Verse 14 says their blood is precious in his sight. Their deaths matter to him. The prayer describes an ideal that no king in the Bible’s history fully met. In 1 Kings 12:4 the people call Solomon’s own rule a heavy yoke.
A changed perspective answers envy

Nothing in the speaker’s circumstances changes at verse 17. Two things change. He stands in a different place, the sanctuary. He looks at a different time, the “end” of the wicked. In verse 15 he says he kept silent to protect others. In verses 21–22 he admits his own bitterness. His answer is finally a presence and not an explanation (verses 23–26).
Ruined worship removes familiar guidance

The poem fits the burning of the temple in 2 Kings 25:9. Verse 9 lists three losses beyond the building. There are no signs, no prophet, and no one who knows how long. The people have lost their guidance. Verse 4 says the enemy set up their own signs there. The people answer by remembering something older than the temple. Verses 12–17 recall God’s power over sea, day, and season.
Judgment interrupts boasting

The idea of “lifting up” runs through verses 4, 5, 6, 7, and 10. The proud lift up their own horn, a picture of an animal’s strength. Verse 6 says promotion comes from no point on the map. Verse 7 gives the true source. God is the judge who lowers and raises. Verse 2 adds that he also sets the time. The boasters control neither the outcome nor the hour.
Broken weapons explain the celebrated power

Verses 3–8 describe a power that stops armies. Verse 3 says God broke the weapons themselves. Verse 8 says the whole earth fell silent. Verse 9 gives the purpose of that power. God rose to judge in order to save the afflicted. The verse says “of the earth,” so the afflicted of every land are meant. The poem celebrates the end of a battle, not the fighting.
Memory answers an unanswered night

Verses 7–9 ask six questions, and none is answered directly. In verse 11 the speaker chooses to remember the exodus. Verse 19 holds the key thought. God made a path through the sea, yet his footprints were not seen. He acted and left no visible track. So a night with no trace of God does not prove he is gone. The poem ends with the flock being led (verse 20).
History becomes instruction for children

Verses 5–6 describe a chain of four generations. Fathers teach children, who teach children not yet born. The lesson they pass on includes Israel’s failures. Verse 8 gives the aim: that they not be like their fathers. History is told here as a warning, not a boast. Verse 7 names three hoped results: hope, memory, and obedience. The long story ends with a shepherd chosen to lead (verses 70–72).
A shattered community appeals through God’s name

Unlike Psalm 44, this prayer admits the people’s sins (verses 8–9). Verse 9 names the ground of their appeal twice. They ask for the glory of God’s name and for his name’s sake. Verse 10 shows what is at stake: nations ask where their God is. So they ask for rescue as mercy and as a defense of God’s honor. Verses 2–3 describe the dead left unburied. That was a deep disgrace.
A vine gives collective loss a form

Verses 8–11 tell Israel’s story as a transplanted vine that flourished. Verse 12 asks why God himself broke down its wall. The gardener has left his own work open to animals. Verse 14 asks him to turn, look, and tend it again. The refrain grows each time it returns (verses 3, 7, 19). God’s title becomes longer and fuller. Isaiah 5:1–7 uses the same picture and gives a reason for the ruin.
Festival praise becomes an appeal to listen

Festival music fills verses 1–3. From verse 6 God’s own voice interrupts it. Verses 9–10 repeat the opening of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2–3). “Open your mouth wide” pictures a young bird waiting to be fed. Verses 11–12 give the sad result. The people’s penalty is to get their own way. Verse 13 begins “Oh that,” which is God’s own longing.
A heavenly courtroom examines earthly injustice

Readers differ on who the “gods” are. Some see heavenly beings, and others see human judges. Jesus quotes verse 6 in John 10:34. Either way, verse 3 states the test of a ruler. He must defend the weak, the poor, and the fatherless. Verse 5 says their failure shakes the foundations of the earth. Verse 8 asks God to take the work over himself.
An enemy list becomes a request for recognition

Verses 6–8 list ten peoples surrounding Israel. Verse 4 states their aim: to erase a nation’s name. Verse 16 states the aim of the prayer. Shame should lead the enemies to seek God’s name. Verse 18 asks that they come to know who he is. Verse 17 still asks for their ruin, and the poem keeps both requests. Even this war prayer hopes its enemies will recognize God.
A threshold receives a different value

The heading gives this poem to the sons of Korah. First Chronicles 9:19 says that family kept the temple gates. So “doorkeeper” in verse 10 is their own post. The lowest job in God’s house is better than a home among the wicked. Verse 3 envies birds that nest near the altar. Verses 5–7 follow travelers on the road there. The verse measures a place by who is present in it.
Remembered restoration leads to another request

The poem moves from past favor to a present plea to listening (verses 1–8). Verses 9–13 describe what the speaker hears. Verse 10 pictures four qualities as people meeting on a road. These often pull apart in human experience. Truth can lack mercy, and peace can ignore what is right. Here they greet each other. Verse 11 adds truth rising from the earth as righteousness looks down.
A plea for help includes a divided heart

Most of the prayer asks for rescue. Verse 11 asks for something inside the speaker. He wants to be taught, and he wants one heart. A heart pulled several ways cannot fear God’s name. Verse 12 then promises thanks “with my whole heart.” Verse 15 quotes God’s own description of himself in Exodus 34:6. The speaker’s request rests on that character.
Birth language expands a city’s people

The nations named in verse 4 include Israel’s old enemies. “Rahab” there is a name for Egypt (Isaiah 30:7). Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, and Philistia fought it for generations. Verse 5 says such people are counted as born in Zion. Verse 6 shows God writing the register himself. Belonging rests on his record, not on birthplace. The poem makes a city’s citizens out of its former foes.
Some prayers end without visible relief

This is the one prayer in the book with no turn toward hope. Its last word is “darkness.” Yet verse 1 calls the LORD “the God of my salvation.” The speaker says three times that he keeps praying (verses 1, 9, 13). His faith shows in the fact that he still speaks. The book of Psalms includes this prayer with the rest. A person may pray this way and still be praying.
A promise becomes grounds for protest

For thirty-seven verses the poet praises a sworn promise. Verse 38 begins, “But you have rejected.” He quotes God’s oath and sets the facts beside it (verses 34–35, 39–45). Verse 49 asks where the sworn kindness has gone. He complains because he believes the promise. The poem gives no answer. A blessing in verse 52 closes the third part of the Psalms.
Counting days leads to a request for lasting work

Verses 3–10 set human life against God’s time. Verse 12 asks to be taught from that contrast. Counting days means knowing they are few. The hoped result is a wise heart. Verses 13–17 then ask for joy to match the years of trouble. The last verse asks twice that their work may last. This poem follows Psalm 89 and looks back before David to God as home.
Protection is spoken through changing voices

Three voices speak in this poem. One says “I” in verse 2, and another addresses “you” in verses 3–13. God speaks as “I” in verses 14–16. Verse 15 is his promise. He will be “with him in trouble,” which assumes trouble comes. The devil quotes verses 11–12 to Jesus in Matthew 4:6. Jesus refuses to use the promise to test God.
Two kinds of growth have different futures

The poem compares two kinds of growth. Verse 7 says the wicked spring up like grass, which does not last. Verse 12 gives the righteous the palm and the cedar. Those trees grow slowly and stand for generations. Verse 14 says they stay green and fruitful in old age. Verse 3 names the lyre among the instruments of this praise. The Egyptian harp shown is a comparison only.
Rising waters meet an established throne

Verse 3 says “lifted up” three times, like water rising. The sea stands for forces no person can control. Verse 4 does not describe a fight. The LORD is simply “on high,” above the breakers. Verse 2 says his throne was in place before the floods rose. Verse 5 turns from the sea to God’s decrees. His firmness is found in teaching that can be trusted.
The prayer names harm made legal

Verses 5–6 name the victims: widows, foreigners, and orphans. Exodus 22:21–22 protected exactly those groups. Verse 7 gives the rulers’ theory that God does not see. Verse 9 answers that the one who made the eye can see. Verse 20 names the worst form of harm. It is done “by statute,” through the law itself. The verse asks whether such a court can claim God’s support.
An invitation changes into a warning

Verses 1–7 are a glad call to worship. In the middle of verse 7 the tone changes. God’s own voice warns the kneeling people. Verse 8 recalls Meribah and Massah (Exodus 17:1–7). Those people had seen God’s works and still tested him. “Today” makes each hearing of God’s voice a new test. The poem ends on the warning and does not soften it.
Creation joins the nations’ song

The circle of singers widens through the poem. It begins with the earth’s peoples (verses 1 and 7). Verses 11–12 add the sky, the sea, the fields, and the trees. Verse 13 gives the reason for their joy. The LORD is coming to judge. Judgment here means setting things right. A world harmed by wrong has reason to sing about that.
Cosmic power leads to a demand about conduct

Verses 2–6 describe fire, lightning, and melting mountains. After that display the poem gives one command. Verse 10 says those who love the LORD must hate evil. Love for God is defined by what a person refuses. The same verse promises that he guards their lives. Verse 11 says light is “sown,” like seed that grows later. The presence that burns enemies in verse 3 gives light to the righteous.
Judgment becomes a reason for music

Three choirs sing in this poem. People play the lyre and trumpets (verses 4–6). The Egyptian harp shown is a comparison for such strings. The sea and its creatures roar (verse 7). Rivers clap and mountains sing (verse 8). Verse 9 gives one reason: the LORD comes to judge with fairness. People who have been wronged can hear that as good news.
Forgiveness and accountability stand together

“Holy” closes each part of the poem (verses 3, 5, 9). Verse 8 shows what that holiness looks like in practice. God answered his servants and forgave them. He also held them to account for what they did. Moses and Aaron are themselves examples. They were forgiven, and they still did not enter the land (Numbers 20:12). The verse keeps mercy and justice together.
Belonging leads into the invitation to enter

The psalm gives seven commands, and “know” stands in the middle. Verse 3 says what there is to know. The LORD made us, so we belong to him. That belonging comes before the call to enter in verse 4. The invitation in verse 1 goes to “all you lands.” Verse 5 gives three reasons for the thanks. The LORD is good, kind, and faithful.
A household becomes a model of public rule

The ruler’s pledge begins at home (verse 2). It then turns to the people he keeps near him. The poem uses “eyes” in two ways. Verse 3 says what he will not look at. Verse 6 says whom he will look for: the faithful of the land. He chooses his servants by their conduct. Verse 8 shows the result reaching the whole city.
A failing life seeks an enduring record

The speaker’s days are short (verses 3, 11, 23). God’s years have no end (verses 12 and 24–27). Verse 18 builds a bridge between the two. His prayer will be written for people not yet created. His words will outlast him even if he does not recover. The poem joins one man’s illness with a ruined city (verses 13–16). Hebrews 1:10–12 quotes verses 25–27.
Mercy takes human limits into account

Verse 13 compares God to a father who pities his children. Verse 14 gives the reason with the word “For.” He knows how humans are formed, and he remembers the dust (Genesis 2:7). A maker’s knowledge leads here to compassion, not contempt. Verses 11–12 measure that mercy by height and by distance. Verses 15–17 set short human life beside lasting kindness. Verse 8 quotes God’s own words about himself from Exodus 34:6.
Creation includes many dependent lives

“These all” in verse 27 covers sea creatures, lions, cattle, and people. Humans are one entry in the list (verses 14–15 and 23). Lions take the night, and people take the day (verses 20–23). They share one world on different shifts. Verse 28 pictures God’s open hand. Verses 29–30 say every breath depends on him. Leviathan appears in verse 26 as a creature at play.
A remembered story changes the meaning of hardship

Genesis 37 says Joseph’s brothers sold him. Verse 17 names another subject: “He sent a man before them.” The poem reads that sale from the end of the story. Verse 18 does not hide the irons on his neck. Verse 19 says the waiting tested him. Joseph gives this reading himself in Genesis 45:5–8. This poem tells only God’s faithful acts, and Psalm 106 tells the other side.
A historical song includes its present singers

Psalm 105 told this history as God’s faithfulness. This poem tells it as Israel’s failure. Verse 6 puts the singers inside the story: “We have sinned with our fathers.” They do not say “they sinned.” Each rebellion in the poem is met by mercy (verses 8, 23, 44–45). Verse 47 shows why they sing it. They are scattered and ask to be gathered.
Repeated rescues invite different groups to answer

Two lines repeat for each group. They cried, and he delivered them (verses 6, 13, 19, 28). Then comes the call to give thanks (verses 8, 15, 21, 31). The travelers and sailors did nothing wrong. The prisoners and the sick brought trouble on themselves (verses 11 and 17). God answers the cry in all four cases. Verse 31 speaks of his deeds for “the children of men.”
A steadfast singer still awaits victory

This poem joins parts of two older ones (57:7–11 and 60:5–12). It leaves out the laments that opened both. Old words are used again for a new need. Verse 7 repeats God’s claim to each region. Verse 11 still admits that he has not marched with the army. The promise is held up while the victory is awaited. The steady heart of verse 1 comes before any change.
The complaint turns failed love into a public case

Verse 4 gives the speaker’s answer to betrayal: he prays. He brings the matter to God as a case. The curses in verses 6–19 are the longest in the Psalms. Some readers take them as his accusers’ words quoted back. The text does not mark them either way. Verse 16 states the charge: this man hunted the poor. Verse 31 sets the LORD at the right hand of the needy.
Royal authority joins another office

The poem contains two sayings from God. Verse 1 gives a throne, and verse 4 gives a priesthood by oath. In Israel kings came from Judah and priests from Levi. King Uzziah was punished for acting as a priest (2 Chronicles 26:18). Melchizedek in Genesis 14:18 was both king and priest before Levi lived. Verse 4 gives the ruler that older kind of office. Hebrews 5–7 applies it to Jesus Christ.
Remembered works lead toward practiced wisdom

Each line of this poem begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Verse 2 says God’s works are to be studied. Verse 4 says they are to be remembered. Verse 5 gives two examples: food and a covenant kept. The poem then moves from works to commands (verse 7). Remembering what God did leads to trusting what he says. Verse 10 calls that the start of wisdom.
A blessed life includes giving away

This poem pairs with Psalm 111 and uses the same alphabet form. Psalm 111 called God gracious and merciful (111:4). Verse 4 here uses those words for the person who fears him. The worshiper comes to resemble the one he worships. His wealth in verse 3 does not stay in his house. He lends in verse 5 and scatters gifts to the poor in verse 9. Second Corinthians 9:9 quotes verse 9.
Great height is expressed through attention below

Verses 4–5 place the LORD above the nations and above the sky. Verse 6 says he must stoop even to see the heavens. From that height he attends to the lowest places. Verse 7 names the dust and the ash heap. Verse 8 seats those people among princes. Verse 9 adds a woman without children. Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel 2:8 uses nearly the same words.
Questions make the landscape a participant

The poem joins two crossings into one event. The sea parts at the exodus, and the Jordan parts at the entry. In verses 5–6 the poet teases the sea, river, and hills with questions. He does not name God until verse 7. Verse 2 says only “his” sanctuary. The delay builds suspense toward the answer. Verse 8 ends with rock turned to water, the reverse of sea turned to land.
Made objects reveal the limits of their makers’ trust

Verses 5–7 go through the idol’s body part by part. Mouth, eyes, ears, nose, hands, feet, and throat all fail. Verse 8 states the cost to the worshiper. People become like what they trust. They grow unable to see, hear, or speak truly. Verse 3 describes the opposite kind of God. He cannot be seen, and he acts.
Gratitude asks what response can be given

Verse 12 asks what a rescued person can give in return. The answer in verse 13 is surprising. He will take a cup, so he receives again. He will also keep calling on the LORD’s name. Verse 14 adds vows kept in public. Gratitude is shown by continued dependence and open thanks. Verse 15 says the death of God’s faithful ones is costly to him.
A very short song has a wide audience

The poem has two verses and the widest audience. Verse 1 speaks to every nation and people. Verse 2 gives the reason, and it is Israel’s own experience. God’s kindness has been great “toward us.” What he did for one people is offered as cause for all to praise. Romans 15:11 quotes verse 1 about the nations joining in.
Rejected value returns in a building image

Builders are the experts, and they judged this stone unfit. Verse 22 says it now holds the chief place. Verse 23 credits the change to the LORD alone. In the poem the stone is the speaker himself. He was near death and now enters the gates (verses 17–20). Jesus quotes verse 22 in Matthew 21:42. The crowd in Matthew 21:9 shouts words from verses 25–26.
Devotion leaves room for being lost

For one hundred seventy-five verses the speaker declares his love for God’s teaching. The last verse is a confession. He has gone astray like a lost sheep. He asks God to seek him. Earlier he said he sought God with his whole heart (verses 2 and 10). Now the seeker needs to be found. Long devotion has not removed his need for rescue, and he still remembers the commands.
Speech begins the songs of ascent amid conflict

Psalms 120–134 carry the heading “A Song of Ascents.” The first one begins far from home. Genesis 10:2 and 25:13 list Meshech and Kedar among other nations. He lives among people who are hostile to him. Verse 7 gives the whole conflict in one line. He speaks for peace, and they answer with war. The journey of these songs starts from not belonging.
The keeper’s wakefulness answers human vulnerability

The words “keep” and “keeper” appear six times in eight verses. The voice changes after verse 2. “I” asks the question, and then someone answers with “you.” Verse 3 names two dangers of a journey. A foot may slip, and a guard may fall asleep. Verse 4 says this guard never does. The remaining verses cover day, night, departure, and return.
Arrival becomes a duty toward the city

The pilgrim arrives in verse 2. Verses 4–5 name what the city is for: worship and justice. Verse 6 then gives the arrival a duty. Those who come must pray for the city’s peace. Verses 8–9 give two reasons. He prays for the sake of his brothers and friends. He prays for the sake of God’s house, and not for his own gain.
Waiting is pictured through directed eyes

Verse 2 compares the people to household servants. A servant watches the master’s hand for a signal or for provision. The verse names both men and women. The word “until” shows the gaze is kept up over time. The trouble in verses 3–4 is not violence. It is contempt from people who live at ease. The people look up to God while others look down on them.
Escape is measured against an imagined alternative

Verses 1–2 begin twice with “If it had not been the LORD.” The poem thanks God by imagining the other outcome. It pictures a beast that swallows (verse 3) and a flood (verses 4–5). Verse 6 pictures teeth that did not close. Verse 7 pictures a bird in a snare. The snare “is broken,” so the escape was not the bird’s skill. The size of the thanks matches what almost happened.
A landscape surrounds a claim of care

Verse 2 draws on the land itself. Jerusalem sits among hills that stand around it. The LORD’s care is pictured as that ring. Verse 3 adds a realistic concern. If wicked rule lasted too long, even good people might give in. So the poem expects a limit on it for their sake. Its trust allows for human weakness.
Remembered joy supports a fresh request

Verses 1–3 remember a past rescue that felt like a dream. Verse 4 says “again,” so more is needed. The Negev is dry land in the south. Its stream beds lie empty and then fill suddenly with rain. Verses 5–6 give a slower picture: seed, waiting, and harvest. A hungry farmer plants grain he could have eaten. The poem asks for both kinds of renewal.
Work has a limit it cannot overcome

Verse 1 does not tell builders and guards to stop working. It says their work alone cannot secure the result. Verse 2 turns to long, anxious hours. Rising early and staying late adds nothing if God does not give. Sleep is named as his gift. “House” can also mean a family, and verses 3–5 turn to children. They too are received, not produced by effort.
A household blessing opens toward public peace

Verse 3 pictures a family meal with two plants. The vine and the olive were the land’s chief crops. Both take years to mature and then bear for a long time. The blessing is slow and lasting, like them. Verses 5–6 widen the view beyond the table. The household’s good is tied to Jerusalem’s good. The last line reaches to all Israel.
A wounded body represents a people’s history

The whole nation speaks here as one person. Verse 3 pictures that person’s back as a plowed field. The furrows are the scars of whipping. “From my youth” reaches back to Egypt. Verse 2 states the result: they “have not prevailed.” Verse 4 says the LORD cut the cords, as one cuts a plow’s harness. Verses 6–8 compare the enemies to rooftop grass that yields no harvest.
Waiting becomes as intense as the approach of dawn

Verse 3 shows that the “depths” include guilt. Verse 4 says forgiveness leads to reverence, not carelessness. Verse 6 compares the speaker to a night watchman. A watchman cannot hurry the dawn, and he knows it will come. The verse says the line twice, which makes the reader wait too. In verse 7 the single voice turns to the whole people. His own waiting becomes advice for Israel.
Quietness receives a bodily image

This poem is three verses long. Verse 1 gives up the need to master things beyond him. Verse 2 describes the result with a child. A weaned child no longer cries for milk. It is content simply to be with its mother. The speaker says, “I have stilled” my soul, so the calm took effort. Verse 3 offers that calm hope to the whole people.
Two acts of choosing connect king and sanctuary

Two oaths stand in this poem. David swears to find a home for the LORD (verses 2–5). The LORD swears to give David a lasting line (verses 11–12). Verse 13 adds a second choice: the LORD has chosen Zion. God’s answer goes beyond what was asked. Verse 9 asks for priests clothed in righteousness. Verse 16 promises salvation, and verse 15 adds bread for the poor.
Unity is described as something spreading

Both pictures in this poem move downward. Oil runs down from head to beard to robe (verse 2). Dew comes down from Hermon to Zion (verse 3). The oil is the priest’s anointing oil of Exodus 30:22–30. It is poured in plenty, not measured out. Hermon stands far north of Zion. So unity is pictured as a gift that arrives from above and beyond.
Blessing travels in both directions

The poem moves in two directions. In verses 1–2 the servants bless the LORD. In verse 3 the LORD blesses “you.” It reads like an exchange of greetings. The servants named work at night, when no crowd is present. The blessing comes from Zion and from the maker of heaven and earth. The songs that began far away in Psalm 120 end inside God’s house.
Memory supplies a contrast with lifeless images

This poem gathers lines from other texts, including Psalm 115:4–8. Its order makes the argument. Verses 5–12 describe a God who acts. He sends weather, strikes Egypt, and gives land. Verse 15 then describes the idols as metal shaped by hands. They have mouths and eyes and do nothing. Verse 14 adds that the LORD has compassion on his servants.
A repeated response binds different acts together

The same reply follows all twenty-six lines. The form fits a leader’s line and a people’s answer. The reply ties very different acts together. Creation, the exodus, and daily food are all called kindness. Verse 23 moves from old history to “us” in our low state. Verse 25 widens to food for “every creature.” The poem ends with thanks to the God of heaven.
Exile changes what a song can do

The captors request music from people who have lost their home. They want Zion’s worship as entertainment. Verse 4 links the LORD’s song with a place and with freedom. The final anger in verses 8–9 must be read beside that loss. Second Kings 25:7 shows what these people had seen. A Babylonian hymn tablet provides a comparison with another tradition of sacred songs. It does not prove that this psalm borrowed from that hymn.
High authority notices low people

The speaker stands among powers: “gods” in verse 1 and kings in verse 4. Verse 6 says where the highest power directs its attention. The LORD is high and looks after the lowly. He keeps the proud at a distance. He knows them “from afar.” Verse 8 holds trust and a request together. God will complete his purpose, and the speaker still asks not to be left.
Being known ends with an invitation to examine

The poem opens with a fact: “you have searched me.” It closes in verse 23 with a request: “Search me.” Between them, being known feels close in more than one way. Verse 5 says he is hemmed in, and verse 7 speaks of fleeing. Verses 13–18 find comfort in it. After fierce words about the wicked in verses 19–22, he turns to himself. Verse 24 asks whether any wicked way is in him.
Speech and violence belong to one threat

Verse 11 names two men together: the slanderer and the violent man. The poem has treated them as one threat throughout. Verses 2–3 describe hearts and tongues. Verses 4–5 describe hands and traps. Verse 11 says evil will “hunt” the violent man. The hunter becomes the hunted. Verse 12 states his confidence that the LORD defends the poor.
The speaker asks protection from joining the harm

Most prayers for protection look outward at enemies. Verse 3 asks for protection from the speaker’s own mouth. Verse 4 adds his heart and his appetite. He fears being drawn in by what the wicked enjoy. The danger is joining them. Verse 5 welcomes correction from a righteous person. He calls such a blow kindness and oil for his head.
A public cry begins in isolation

A defender stood at a person’s right hand (see 109:31). In verse 4 that place is empty. He says refuge has fled and no one cares. Verse 5 answers the empty place: “You are my refuge.” The LORD is also his share among the living. The poem begins in isolation. Its last verse expects the righteous to gather around him.
A plea for rescue includes a limit on judgment

The speaker wants rescue from an enemy. Verse 2 makes clear he does not ask on his own merit. No living person could stand in that court. He appeals instead to God’s faithfulness (verse 1) and name (verse 11). He then asks four times to be guided or taught (verses 8 and 10). Rescue alone is not all he wants. Romans 3:20 echoes verse 2.
A war prayer turns toward ordinary flourishing

The poem begins as a king’s prayer in wartime. Verse 12 shows what the fighting is for. The goal is ordinary life at home. Sons grow like healthy plants, and daughters stand like carved pillars. Verses 13–14 add full barns, large flocks, and quiet streets. Verse 14 names no breach, no exile, and no outcry. Peace is described in things people can see.
Kingship becomes visible through provision

The word “all” or “every” runs through this poem. Verses 11–13 speak of God’s kingdom and power. Verses 14–16 show what that kingship looks like. He lifts those who fall and feeds every living thing. Verse 16 pictures an open hand. The king is known by what he provides. This is the last poem in the book that carries David’s name.
Human mortality limits political trust

Verse 3 does not say that rulers are wicked. Verse 4 gives the reason for the warning. A ruler’s breath leaves him, and his plans end that day. Hope placed in him ends with him. Verse 6 sets God’s lasting faithfulness against that. Verses 7–9 list what a good ruler should do. The LORD does each one for the hungry, the prisoner, and the stranger.
City rebuilding and healing share one hymn

Verse 2 speaks of a city rebuilt and outcasts gathered. Verse 3 turns to hearts that are broken. Verse 4 turns to the number of the stars. The poem sets these side by side without comment. The one who names every star also binds wounds. Verses 10–11 say military strength does not impress him. The word that melts ice is the word given to Israel (verses 18–19).
A list removes rank from the invitation

The list moves from the heavens down to the earth (verses 1–6, 7–12). People come last. Among people verse 11 names kings and rulers first. Verse 12 then names young men and women, old men and children. Rank gives no better place in this choir. Snow and sea creatures are called before any king. Verse 13 gives the reason: only his name is exalted.
Celebration carries a forceful second movement

The poem turns sharply at verse 6. Dancing and song give way to a sword. Verse 9 limits what the sword may do. It carries out “the written judgment,” so it is not private revenge. Verse 4 says the people honored this way are the humble. The text joins worship and judgment and does not explain how. Readers have understood the time and manner in different ways.
Praise includes bodies, skills, and many sounds

The poem answers four questions in order. Verse 1 says where, and verse 2 says why. Verses 3–5 say how, and verse 6 says who. Verses 3–5 name trumpet, strings, drums, dancing, flute, and cymbals. An Egyptian harp shows one ancient form of a string instrument. Praise uses breath, hands, skill, and the whole body. The book began with one blessed person and ends with everything that breathes.
